claim: Measured by the whole WSTS market, the AI wave's growth so far is similar in pace to the mid-1990s PC boom but far larger in dollars: the market grew 51% from 2023 to 2025 (US$526.9bn to US$795.6bn, +US$269bn), versus 141% over 1992-1995 (US$59.9bn to US$144.4bn, +US$84bn) and 37% in the single year 2000.
notes: Uses CLM-0030, CLM-0599, CLM-0602, CLM-0606, CLM-0607, CLM-0630. Nominal USD, not inflation-adjusted. 2023 was a cyclical trough, flattering the AI-wave growth rate; the 1995 and 2000 peaks were followed by declines (1996 -8.6%, 2001 -32%).

claim: Unlike the PC and smartphone waves, which lifted broad product categories, the AI wave's gains are concentrated in a few firms: NVIDIA's annual Data Center revenue alone rose by about US$179bn between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, comparable to the whole WSTS market's US$269bn increase over 2023-2025.
evidence: Reading of NVIDIA Data Center claims in this batch against WSTS CLM-0030 and CLM-0630; supported by Omdia estimate CLM-0721 (Nvidia, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron rose from 24% to 42% of chip revenue 2023-2025).
notes: NVIDIA Data Center revenue includes systems, networking and software, not only chips, and uses a fiscal year ending January; the comparison is indicative, not additive.

claim: A like-for-like comparison of the AI wave with the PC and smartphone waves by end-use segment (chip revenue attributable to PCs in the 1990s or smartphones in 2010-2015) could not be built from free data, because the WSTS End Use Survey history and product splits before 2020 are not public.
evidence: Checked existing WSTS claims (CLM-0591: free WSTS history is regional only) and SIA end-use claims (CLM-0560, 2024 only); no public time series of chip demand by end use for 1990-2015 was found.
